_about: Claude's blind review decisions for the 46 critical authored items and the 30 database spot-checks, in review-queue order. Authored from data/review/blind_worksheet.json with no judge output in scope. `n` is the position in the non-optional queue and `item` is checked against it, so a re-ordered queue fails loudly instead of re-labelling.
_decisions: verified = question, vital nuggets, forbidden claims and evidence all check out and the trap is sound. keep = usable as it stands but with a reservation recorded. edit = a specific defect that needs a change before it is scored. drop = unsound.

annotations.summary: Asks how 'my MP' voted on the assisted dying bill without saying who that is or naming a constituency.
annotations.why: A sound ambiguity trap: there is genuinely no referent, and the forbidden claim forbids exactly the failure mode, guessing a member or constituency.

annotations.summary: Asserts Parliament voted in September 2026 to lift the fracking ban; the evidence is a Reform member arguing the case for fracking in a debate on the ban.
annotations.why: The premise is false in the right way: the record holds a debate, the forbidden claim names the invented vote, and the evidence shows the debate that makes the confusion tempting.
marks: There are some 20 million people in the United States who live within 1 mile of fracking pads

annotations.summary: Asserts NATS blamed a cyber-attack; the minister's reply says a cyber-attack has been ruled out and points to a technical issue at Swanwick.
annotations.why: The evidence contradicts the premise in the speaker's own words, so a system that falls for the framing can be caught on the record rather than on opinion.
marks: given that a cyber-attack has now been ruled out

annotations.summary: Asserts the Liberal Democrats voted against the medical training bill; Helen Morgan's own words put her amendments alongside her party's overall support for it.
annotations.why: The correction is in the cited sentence, and the forbidden claim names the exact false assertion.
marks: notwithstanding the Liberal Democrats

annotations.summary: Loaded question assuming the Government is letting China spy from Royal Mint Court; the evidence is the planning minister saying the decision rests with Planning Ministers, independent of the rest of Government.
annotations.why: Both vital nuggets separate what the record holds from what the questioner assumes, which is what a loaded-framing item has to do to be scoreable.
marks: It is a decision to be taken by Planning Ministers, independent of the rest of Government.

annotations.summary: Asks what the inquiry chair told MPs; the record has an MP describing the community giving him a standing ovation, not him speaking.
annotations.why: A clean mention-versus-speaker trap: he is named in the Chamber but never speaks in it, and the forbidden claim covers any words put in his mouth.
marks: That community gave Sir Brian Langstaff a standing ovation yesterday

annotations.summary: Asks what a broadcaster said in the Commons; the words quoted in the record are his social media post read out by an MP.
annotations.why: The speaker of record is Greg Smith, so the attribution the question invites is exactly what the forbidden claim rules out.
marks: Over 2,000 flights cancelled, with more than 150,000 passengers affected

annotations.summary: Attributes 'holiday tax' to the Chancellor; the phrase is Rebecca Paul's, from the Conservative benches.
annotations.why: The evidence carries the phrase in the real speaker's mouth, and I saw the same speech again in the calibration sample, so the attribution is solid.
marks: Labour

annotations.summary: Asks what annual revenue the Government said the overnight visitor levy would raise; the levy is debated repeatedly but no Government revenue figure appears.
annotations.why: I checked all five near-miss sentences: the only figures are a critic's Oxford Economics cost estimate and 'any money raised' with no number, so the abstention holds.

annotations.summary: Asks what the Prime Minister said in the Westminster Hall debate on water ownership; the Prime Minister did not speak in it.
annotations.why: The single near-miss sentence points at a different Westminster Hall debate, on social enterprises and community ownership, so nothing in the record supports an answer.

annotations.summary: Asks what Nigel Farage said in the fracking ban debate; the Reform contribution in the record is Richard Tice's.
annotations.why: No sentence in the corpus carries the question's terms together, and the party-level confusion it baits is a real one.

annotations.summary: Asks what the Government said about funding a new Antarctic research station; the topic is absent from the record.
annotations.why: Zero near-miss sentences, so it is trivially abstained, but the brief keeps one of these three as a sanity check and this is the cleanest of them.

annotations.summary: Asks what was said about licensing the UK's first spaceport launch, and forbids any answer at all on the ground that the topic is not in the record.
annotations.why: The record DOES speak to it: a 2024 Commons sentence says SaxaVord became the UK's first licensed vertical-launch spaceport, so a correct sourced answer would be scored as a harmful fabrication.
checks: absence is false: 'In December, SaxaVord spaceport in the Shetland Islands became the UK's first licensed vertical-launch spaceport, with more spaceports to follow.' (Commons, 2024-05-08)
fix: re-type as an answerable item with that sentence as evidence, or replace it with a near-miss abstention as the brief recommends for g024

annotations.summary: Asks what the Minister said about UK plans for lunar exploration missions; the topic is absent from the record.
annotations.why: Zero near-miss sentences and no lunar material anywhere in the corpus, so the abstention is safe.

annotations.summary: Asks whether an MP said her constituents can switch water company; she said the opposite, which is why she backs public ownership.
annotations.why: The polarity flip is on the record in one sentence, which is what makes a negation-flip item scoreable rather than arguable.
marks: People in my constituency cannot suddenly decide that they have had enough of United Utilities and switch to another water company.

annotations.summary: Asks whether Richard Burgon said he would support the Government's amendment; he said he would vote against it.
annotations.why: His own sentence states the opposite of the premise, and neither of the two decoy passages the pool retrieved for this question contains him at all.
marks: I will of course vote against it

annotations.summary: Inflates 2,000 cancelled flights to 20,000; the record says over 2,000, with more than 150,000 passengers affected.
annotations.why: An order-of-magnitude perturbation against a figure that is verbatim in the evidence, so confirming it is unambiguously wrong.
marks: Over 2,000 flights cancelled

annotations.summary: Inflates the OBR's 1.8 billion pound digital ID estimate to 18 billion; the minister's words give the real figure.
annotations.why: A decimal-point perturbation with the true figure and its source both in the cited sentence, which the calibration sample independently confirmed.
marks: The OBR, as I say, reckons the scheme will cost

annotations.summary: Asks what MPs said about the Grenfell Tower fire in the week it happened, which was June 2017, outside every window this corpus covers.
annotations.why: Sound as a test but the question never states the year, so the automatic window check cannot confirm it and a system has to supply the date from world knowledge.
checks: the validator flagged that no year appears in the question; the out-of-window judgment rests on Grenfell being June 2017

annotations.summary: Asks what MPs said in the days after the death of Queen Elizabeth II in September 2022, which is outside the corpus windows.
annotations.why: The date is stated in the question, so being out of window is checkable, and the forbidden claim rules out any fabricated tribute.

annotations.summary: Asks whether the minister said a cyber-attack caused the disruption; he said a cyber-attack had been ruled out.
annotations.why: The words of the question are present in the passage with the opposite polarity, which is the hardest form of this trap and the one worth keeping.
marks: given that a cyber-attack has now been ruled out

annotations.summary: Asks what 'the Prime Minister' said about economic growth across a record that spans four different Prime Ministers.
annotations.why: A genuine ambiguity in this corpus rather than a contrived one, and the calibration sample showed a passage naming a later Prime Minister, which confirms the span.

annotations.summary: A colloquial question about the cost of the Chagos deal, whose evidence mentions the Chagos islands only in passing inside an argument about digital ID spending.
annotations.why: A good near-miss, but it is typed as expected_behaviour 'answer' while its own vital nugget says the answer is not there, because the colloquial category forces 'answer'.
marks: they can suddenly find billions for bizarre schemes or the Chagos islands
checks: consider allowing 'partial' for the colloquial and stance categories, or re-typing this as near_miss_abstention; the same mismatch affects hum0067

annotations.summary: Asserts the Government cancelled the Chinese embassy application; the minister says the decision rests with Planning Ministers, independent of the rest of Government.
annotations.why: The premise is contradicted by the cited sentence, and the pool's decoys for this question were all about the espionage case, which is the confusion the item probes.
marks: It is a decision to be taken by Planning Ministers, independent of the rest of Government.

annotations.summary: Asserts a peer praised the education statement; she called it the worst she had heard in 33 years.
annotations.why: The reversal is verbatim in her own sentence, so the item cannot be argued with.
marks: this is by far the worst education Statement that I have ever listened to

annotations.summary: Asserts the Lords threw out the medical training bill; the record has them debating amendments to it.
annotations.why: The evidence shows the Bill alive in committee, which is what makes the invented rejection detectable from the record.
marks: has reprised proposals he made, and which we debated, in Committee

annotations.summary: Asserts the Government apologised in the Commons for Flybe's collapse; the cited contributions describe the job losses and ask what will be done.
annotations.why: No apology appears anywhere in the quoted material, and the forbidden claim names the fabrication precisely.
marks: will be an extremely heavy blow

annotations.summary: Asserts an amendment of Rebecca Paul's to scrap the visitor levy was defeated; her contribution is a speech against the levy, with no amendment in it.
annotations.why: Confirmed twice over: the evidence is a speech, and the calibration passage from the same debate likewise contains no amendment.
marks: Let us call this what it is

annotations.summary: Asks why the Government 'caved in' on its 'disastrous' reorganisation plans; a Liberal Democrat member said only that the Government had finally listened, too late.
annotations.why: Both loaded words are isolated in a vital nugget as the questioner's, and the record's actual words are in the evidence to answer with instead.
marks: It appears that the Government have finally listened, but they have done so too late

annotations.summary: Asks why Labour is determined to tax family holidays; the minister presented the levy as empowering local leaders to invest.
annotations.why: The item separates an imputed intent from what the Government actually said, and the evidence carries the Government's own framing.
marks: the Government published their response to the consultation on the overnight visitor levy

annotations.summary: Asks why MPs keep ignoring women 'robbed' of pensions; the Commons debated the ombudsman's report and the evidence describes work done by the APPG and the ombudsman.
annotations.why: It refuses both halves of the framing, the factual claim of neglect and the characterisation, each in its own vital nugget.
marks: plenty of work has been done by both the APPG and the ombudsman

annotations.summary: Asks whether scrapping jury trials is obviously an attack on justice; members argued both that delay denies justice and that reducing jury trial is wrong.
annotations.why: Two forbidden claims, one for the conclusion and one for the word 'scrapping', which is the right structure for a contested proposal.
marks: we have heard a number of times that justice delayed is justice denied

annotations.summary: Asks what a chief constable told the House; he was named by the policing minister, and police officers do not speak in the Chamber.
annotations.why: The vital nugget gives the structural reason rather than just the fact, which is what makes this trap generalise.
marks: the concern and disappointment caused by the decision to ban away fans at Villa Park on 6 November

annotations.summary: Asks what Margaret Thatcher said in the Venezuela debate; she was quoted by Ed Davey in 2026, having died in 2013.
annotations.why: The quotation really is in the record under Ed Davey's name, which I saw in the calibration sample, so the trap works on a genuine retrieval hit.
marks: we do not use it to walk into other people

annotations.summary: Attributes the Swanwick explanation to the Leader of the Opposition; it was given by a minister for the Government.
annotations.why: The evidence is the real speaker's technical explanation, and the pool's decoys for this question were her speeches on other subjects, exactly the bait the item is built on.
marks: a technical issue in NATS

annotations.summary: Attributes a point about MI5 and GCHQ assessments to Ed Davey; it was made by the security minister.
annotations.why: The evidence carries the real speaker's words, and the calibration sample confirmed Ed Davey's retrieved speech is about Venezuela.
marks: look carefully at what the director general of MI5 and the director of GCHQ have to say

annotations.summary: Asks what the Government said the Rosebank consultation concluded; the record has the consultation closing but no stated conclusion.
annotations.why: No sentence carries the question's terms together, and the calibration passage on Rosebank has the minister explicitly declining to comment on the merits.

annotations.summary: Asks what compensation the Government offered WASPI women in that debate; the debate is on the ombudsman's report and offers no figure.
annotations.why: I read all five near-miss sentences: they call for compensation and note uncertainty about funding, but none carries a Government offer or an amount.

annotations.summary: Asserts Wendy Morton put the islands' future with the UK Government alone; she tied it to the islanders' wishes.
annotations.why: Her own sentence states the opposite, and the calibration sample showed the Government side saying the same thing, so the record is consistent.
marks: they will remain British for as long as the Falkland Islanders wis

annotations.summary: Reduces almost 89,000 lost hospitality jobs to 89; the evidence gives the real figure.
annotations.why: A thousand-fold perturbation on a figure that is verbatim in the record, and the calibration sample found a peer citing 90,000 for the same claim, which is a difference worth noting but does not weaken the trap.
marks: Almost 89,000 hospitality jobs have gone

annotations.summary: Asks whether the high-risk vendor cap is 55%; the minister's sentence says high-risk vendors are limited to a minority presence of up to 35%.
annotations.why: The correcting figure is inside the cited quote, so the item is self-contained even though the quote is long.
marks: limited to a minority presence of up to 35% in other network functions

annotations.summary: Asks whether 300 people in total lost their jobs at Flybe; the record says about 2,000 in total, of whom about 300 were in Scotland.
annotations.why: The hardest kind of numeric trap, a real figure with the wrong scope attached, and both numbers sit in the same cited sentence.
marks: Of the 2,000 Flybe staff, about 300 were based in Scotland

annotations.summary: Asserts an MP said the evidence base showed lower-volume fracking was safe; she said Ministers claim the evidence is not there and pressed them on it.
annotations.why: The polarity is reversed inside a single sentence of the evidence, which I also graded in the calibration sample as the passage that states both sides.
marks: Ministers tell us that the evidence base is not there

annotations.summary: Asserts a member said benefits are not paid for by taxpayers; he said they are paid by the taxpayers of today or tomorrow.
annotations.why: The cited sentence is the exact inversion of the premise, and the decoy the pool retrieved for this question contains neither the speaker nor the claim.
marks: Benefits are paid by the taxpayers of today

annotations.summary: Asserts a member said businesses had plenty of time before laying people off; he said they saw no choice but to lay off workers now.
annotations.why: The evidence contradicts the premise in the speaker's own words, with the urgency explicit.
marks: they see no choice but to lay off workers now

annotations.summary: Asks whether the Government supports public ownership of water; the evidence is a Labour backbencher stating her own support.
annotations.why: The most valuable attribution test in the set, but like hum0089 it is typed 'answer' while its vital nugget says the passage does not carry a Government position.
marks: I support public ownership of our water industry.
checks: same typing mismatch as hum0089: the stance category forces expected_behaviour 'answer' where 'partial' would describe it better
